entry: Emperor of Russia, King of Poland and Grand Duke of Finland (r. 1855–81). Known as Alexander the Liberator for the Edict of Emancipation of 1861, which abolished [[Serfdom|serfdom]] in the [[Russian Empire]], he also introduced judicial reforms, relaxed media censorship and promoted local self-government. Many of these reforms were later cut back, and he became more conservative after an assassination attempt in 1866. He sold Alaska to the United States in 1867, having backed the Union in the [[American Civil War]]. Russian forces won the [[Russo-Turkish War (1877–1878)|Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878]], which secured the independence of Bulgaria, Montenegro, Romania and Serbia from the [[Ottoman Empire]]. After the Polish uprising of 1863 he abolished Poland's separate constitution and incorporated the kingdom directly into the empire. He was killed in [[Saint Petersburg]] by a bomb thrown by members of the Narodnaya Volya organization.

Emperor of Russia (r. 1801–25), first King of Congress Poland and Grand Duke of Finland. He ruled during the [[Napoleonic Wars]]. Early in his reign he introduced minor reforms and appointed the reformer Mikhail Speransky as an adviser, but plans for a parliament and a constitution were never realized. He changed Russia's stance toward [[Napoleon]] several times between 1804 and 1812. After defeats at Austerlitz and Friedland he allied with Napoleon by the Treaty of Tilsit in 1807, and he took Finland from [[Sweden]] in 1809. Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812 ended in catastrophe for the French, and Alexander later formed the Holy Alliance to suppress revolutionary movements. In the second half of his reign he grew increasingly reactionary and dismissed Speransky. He died of [[Typhus]] while traveling in southern Russia and was succeeded by his brother [[Nicholas I of Russia|Nicholas I]], after a confused interval that preceded the Decembrist revolt.

Island in the Bellingshausen Sea, the largest island of [[Antarctica]] and the second-largest uninhabited island in the world, after Devon Island. It lies west of the [[Antarctic Peninsula]], from which it is separated by Marguerite Bay and George VI Sound. Discovered on January 28, 1821, by a Russian expedition under Fabian Gottlieb von Bellingshausen, it was named Alexander I Land for [[Alexander I of Russia|Tsar Alexander I]]. It was thought to be part of the mainland until a two-person sledge party from the United States Antarctic Service proved in 1940 that it was an island. The United Kingdom claimed it in 1908, and [[Chile]] and [[Argentina]] later made claims, but under the Antarctic Treaty none has been officially recognized. Hodgson Lake, a former subglacial lake, lay under an ice sheet at least 470 m thick during the [[Last Glacial Maximum]] and has been sealed beneath perennial ice since before 11,000 years ago.

Prince of Novgorod and Grand Prince of Vladimir (1252–63). He won a victory over Swedish invaders at the Battle of the Neva in 1240, which earned him the title Nevsky, and over German crusaders at the Battle on the Ice in 1242. He paid tribute to the [[Golden Horde]], which allowed him to preserve the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]] while fighting foreign powers to the west and south. The [[Russian Orthodox Church]] canonized him in 1547. [[Peter the Great]] used his image in the construction of [[Saint Petersburg]], and the [[Soviet Union]] promoted him as a symbol of patriotism during [[World War II]]. Critics argue that the size of his victories was exaggerated for political purposes and that he helped ensure the Golden Horde's dominance over Russia.

Russian [[Ice hockey|ice hockey]] left winger and captain of the Washington Capitals of the [[National Hockey League]]. He has scored more regular-season goals than any other player in NHL history, and he is the only player to have reached 900. The Capitals selected him first overall in 2004, and he won the Hart Memorial Trophy as most valuable player three times. He also won the Maurice Richard Trophy as league-leading goal scorer a record nine times. In 2018 the Capitals won their first Stanley Cup, and he was named playoff MVP.

English poet, translator and satirist of the Augustan era. Born in London to Catholic parents, he was largely self-educated because the Test Acts, which upheld the status of the [[Church of England]], barred Catholics from universities and public office. He read [[Horace]], [[Virgil]], [[Homer]] and [[Geoffrey Chaucer]], and later translated Homer's [[Iliad]]. Pott disease, a form of [[Tuberculosis]] of the spine, deformed his body and left him only 4 feet 6 inches tall. His best-known works are the satirical *An Essay on Criticism* (1711), *The Rape of the Lock* (1712–1717) and *The Dunciad* (1728–1743). Lines such as "damning with faint praise" and "to err is human; to forgive, divine" have entered common use.

Russian poet, playwright and novelist of the Romantic era, regarded as the greatest Russian poet and the founder of modern [[Russian literature]]. Born into the nobility in [[Moscow]], he was a grandson of a maternal line that included Abram Petrovich Gannibal, a general born near [[Lake Chad]] in present-day [[Cameroon]] who had been kidnapped by the Ottomans and freed by [[Peter the Great]]. Several of his poems, including "Ode to Liberty", led to his exile. Under strict surveillance and unable to publish, he wrote the play *Boris Godunov*, and his verse novel *Eugene Onegin* was serialized between 1825 and 1832. He was fatally wounded in a [[Duel|duel]] with Georges-Charles de Heeckeren d'Anthès, a French officer in the Russian service whom he believed to be his wife's lover.

Russian general and military theorist, known as Prince of Italy. He fought in the [[Seven Years' War]] and the Russo-Turkish wars, winning decisive victories at Kozludzha and Rymnik and storming Izmail. In 1794 he put down the Polish uprising, defeating the insurgents at Praga. His tactics stressed speed, [[Bayonet|bayonet]] assaults and rigorous training. In the [[French Revolutionary Wars]] he commanded the Austro-Russian army, captured [[Milan]] and [[Turin]], and nearly erased [[Napoleon]]'s Italian conquests. Cut off in Switzerland, he extracted his army from the Alps and was promoted to generalissimo. He wrote *The Science of Victory*, which stressed offensive action and rapid maneuver. Undefeated in major engagements, he is considered the greatest military commander in Russian history.

German [[Polymath|polymath]], geographer, naturalist and explorer. Between 1799 and 1804 he traveled extensively in the [[Americas]] with the French explorer Aimé Bonpland, identifying the source of the [[Orinoco]] River and in 1802 climbing the highest mountain in Ecuador, then a record altitude for a Westerner. With Carl Ritter he is regarded as a founder of modern [[Geography]], and his quantitative work on botanical geography laid foundations for biogeography. His multivolume treatise *Kosmos* sought to unify scientific knowledge and presented the universe as one interacting entity, introducing concepts of ecology. He described local human-induced [[Climate change]] in 1800 and again in 1831. Often called the father of ecology and of environmentalism, he promoted scientific internationalism.

French novelist and playwright. His historical adventure novels, many first published as serials, include *The Count of Monte Cristo* and *The Three Musketeers*, and he is one of the most widely read French authors. He began his career with plays, which were successfully produced from the first, and his published works total 100,000 pages, including magazine articles and travel books. In the 1840s he founded the Théâtre Historique in Paris. His father, General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas, was born in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, now [[Haiti]], to a French nobleman and an enslaved woman. After Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte's election in 1851, Dumas fell from favor and spent several years in Belgium, Russia and Italy. In 1861 he founded the newspaper *L'Indépendant*, which supported Italian unification, and he returned to Paris in 1864.

Port city (pop., 2024: 5,700,000) on the Mediterranean coast of northern [[Egypt]], at the western edge of the [[Nile]] Delta. Founded by [[Alexander the Great]] in 331 BC on the site of an earlier Egyptian settlement, it became the capital of the [[Ptolemaic Kingdom]] and a leading center of learning in the Hellenistic age and late antiquity, when it was at one time the most populous city in the ancient world. Its Great Library was the largest in antiquity, and the Pharos [[Lighthouse]] was one of the [[Seven Wonders of the Ancient World]]. Egypt's capital until Fustat, now part of [[Cairo]], was founded, Alexandria was a major hub of early Christianity. It is today the country's principal seaport and second-largest city.

Russian opposition leader, anti-corruption activist and political prisoner. He founded the Anti-Corruption Foundation in 2011 to expose alleged official corruption. Twice given suspended sentences for embezzlement, he was barred from the 2018 presidential election. In August 2020 he was poisoned with the Novichok nerve agent and treated in [[Berlin]], and he accused [[Vladimir Putin]] of responsibility. Back in Russia from 2021, he was imprisoned and given further sentences on extremism charges. Russian officials cited natural causes for his reported death; a 2026 joint statement by five European governments asserted that he had been poisoned with epibatidine, a toxin from [[Poison dart frog|South American poison dart frogs]].

Spanish footballer from [[Catalonia]], a midfielder or forward. She won eight league titles and four UEFA Women's Champions League trophies with Barcelona, and captained the club to a continental quadruple in 2025–26. She won the Ballon d'Or Féminin in 2021, 2022 and 2026, and was part of Spain's victory at the [[FIFA Women's World Cup]] in 2023. She holds the record for most appearances for the Spain women's national team.

French diplomat, political philosopher and historian. He is best known for *Democracy in America* (1835 and 1840), based on his travels in the United States, and for *The Old Regime and the Revolution* (1856). The first is considered an early work of sociology and [[Political science|political science]]. He analyzed the role of [[Voluntary association|voluntary associations]] and warned of the "tyranny of the majority". A [[Liberalism|liberal]] who advocated parliamentary government, he sat in the lower house from 1839 to 1851, supporting abolitionism and free trade while backing the colonization of Algeria. In *The Old Regime and the Revolution* he argued that the [[French Revolution]] continued the centralization of the state begun under [[Louis XIV]]. He retired from politics after Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte's coup of December 2, 1851.

Tsar of all Russia (r. 1645–76) and the second ruler of the [[House of Romanov]]. He was the first tsar to sign laws on his own authority, and the Sobornoye Ulozheniye law code of 1649 strengthened the bonds between autocracy and the lower nobility while binding peasants more firmly to the land. After a Salt Riot in Moscow in 1648 he was forced to exile his tutor, the boyar Boris Morozov. Alexis backed Patriarch Nikon's liturgical reforms, which provoked a schism in the [[Russian Orthodox Church]] and the persecution of the [[Old Believers]]. Under the Treaty of Pereyaslavl in 1654 with Cossack leader [[Bohdan Khmelnytsky]], Russia gained left-bank Ukraine, and wars with Poland, Sweden and Iran followed. At his death Russia spanned almost 8.1 million km2.

Mexican filmmaker, director, screenwriter and producer. His breakthrough was the coming-of-age film *Y tu mamá también* (2001). He went on to direct *Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban* (2004), the dystopian *Children of Men* (2006), the science fiction drama *Gravity* (2013) and the semi-autobiographical *Roma* (2018). His accolades include four [[Academy Awards]], among them Best Director for both *Gravity* and *Roma*, and Best Film Editing for *Gravity* and Best Cinematography for *Roma*.

English filmmaker, known as the Master of Suspense. He entered the film industry in 1919 as a title card designer, and *The Lodger* (1927) was his first successful film, helping to shape the thriller genre. His British thrillers *The 39 Steps* (1935) and *The Lady Vanishes* (1938) are ranked among the greatest British films of the 20th century. After moving to Hollywood in 1939 he directed *Rebecca* (1940), which won the Academy Award for Best Picture. He worked with [[Cary Grant]], [[James Stewart]], [[Ingrid Bergman]] and [[Grace Kelly]], and his films include *Shadow of a Doubt* (1943), *Vertigo* (1958), *North by Northwest* (1959) and *Psycho* (1960). In 2012 *Vertigo* displaced [[Citizen Kane]] as the British Film Institute's greatest film in its critics' poll. He hosted the television anthology *Alfred Hitchcock Presents*.

American sexologist, biologist and professor of entomology and [[Zoology|zoology]]. Originally a specialist in gall wasps at Indiana University, he turned to human sexuality in the 1930s and in 1947 founded the Institute for Sex Research there, now the Kinsey Institute. He is best known for *Sexual Behavior in the Human Male* (1948) and *Sexual Behavior in the Human Female* (1953), known as the Kinsey Reports, and for the Kinsey scale. The reports sold widely and influenced social and cultural values in the United States and United Kingdom, but critics have argued that their sampling was not random and overrepresented prisoners and sex offenders. His work on [[Human sexuality|human sexuality]] remains controversial. Rickets and other childhood illnesses left him with a stoop that kept him from being drafted for [[World War I]].

Swedish chemist, inventor, engineer and businessman. Born in [[Stockholm]], he moved with his family to [[Saint Petersburg]] in the [[Russian Empire]] after his father was forced into [[Bankruptcy|bankruptcy]], and his father prospered there making machine tools and [[Explosive|explosives]]. Nobel's most famous invention, [[Dynamite|dynamite]], was an explosive made from [[Nitroglycerin|nitroglycerin]] and patented in 1867; he further invented gelignite and ballistite and held 355 patents. He bequeathed his fortune to a foundation that funds the [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prizes]], awarded annually to those who have "conferred the greatest benefit to mankind". The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences chooses the laureates in physics and chemistry. He also wrote poetry in English and the prose tragedy *Nemesis*.

English mathematician, logician and philosopher. With his former student [[Bertrand Russell]] he wrote the three-volume *Principia Mathematica* (1910–1913), one of the most important works in [[Mathematical logic]] of the 20th century. From the late 1910s he turned from mathematics to the [[Philosophy of science|philosophy of science]] and then to [[Metaphysics]], developing process philosophy, which holds that reality consists of processes defined by their relations rather than of independent bits of matter. His *Process and Reality* (1929) is regarded as the foundational text of the school, which has been applied in ecology, theology, education, physics, biology, economics and psychology. He taught at [[Cambridge]] and University College London before joining [[Harvard University]] in 1924 as professor of philosophy.

English naturalist, explorer, geographer and anthropologist. He independently conceived the theory of evolution by [[Natural selection|natural selection]]; his 1858 paper on the subject was published alongside extracts from [[Charles Darwin]]'s writings, which prompted Darwin to publish an abstract of his work as [[On the Origin of Species]] in 1859. Fieldwork in the Amazon basin and the [[Malay Archipelago]] led him to identify the faunal divide now called the Wallace Line, which separates the largely Asian fauna of western [[Indonesia]] from the Australasian fauna of the east. Considered the leading expert of his century on the geographical distribution of animals, he is called the father of biogeography. Late in life he became a socialist, and his advocacy of spiritualism and [[Mind–body dualism|mind–body dualism]] strained his relations with other scientists.

Polish-American logician and mathematician, best known for his work on model theory, metamathematics and the concept of [[Truth|truth]]. Born Alfred Teitelbaum to Polish-Jewish parents, he earned a doctorate at the University of [[Warsaw]] in 1924 and taught in Poland until 1939, when he emigrated to the United States. His 1933 Polish monograph defined truth for formalized languages. He also contributed to [[Abstract algebra|abstract algebra]], [[Topology|topology]], [[Geometry|geometry]] and [[Set theory|set theory]]. He taught at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] from 1942 until his death, and in 1958 founded a group in logic and the methodology of science there. His biographers state that he and [[Kurt Gödel]] changed the face of logic in the twentieth century.

German climatologist, meteorologist and polar researcher. He pioneered the use of weather balloons, with his brother Kurt, to track [[Air mass|air masses]], and made several expeditions to [[Greenland]] to study polar air circulation. Today he is best remembered as the originator of the theory of continental drift, which he presented in 1912 and set out in *The Origin of Continents and Oceans* (1915). He argued that the continents had once formed the supercontinent [[Pangaea]] and had slowly drifted apart, citing matching coastlines, fossils and rock formations. Mainstream geology rejected the idea largely for lack of a driving mechanism until discoveries such as palaeomagnetism supported it from the 1960s, when it became the basis of [[Plate tectonics]]. He died on his final Greenland expedition.

King of [[Wessex]] (r. 871–899) and of the [[Anglo-Saxons]]. The youngest son of King Æthelwulf, he spent his early reign fighting [[Vikings]], winning a decisive victory at the Battle of Edington in 878. He then agreed to divide England between Anglo-Saxon territory and the Viking-ruled Danelaw, and oversaw the conversion of the Viking leader Guthrum to Christianity. In 886, after retaking London from the Vikings, he began styling himself King of the Anglo-Saxons. He introduced administrative and military reforms, established a court school for nobles and commoners, and had Latin works translated into [[Old English]]. He is the only native-born English monarch to be labeled the Great, an epithet popularized from the 16th century.

Argentine-born Spanish footballer and manager who played as a forward, nicknamed the Blond Arrow. He played in all five of the [[Madrid|Real Madrid]] European Cup victories of the 1950s and 1960s and scored 216 league goals for the club, a record at the time. After a footballers' strike in Argentina in 1949 he played for Millonarios of [[Bogotá]] in Colombia until 1953. He won the Ballon d'Or in 1957 and 1959, and in 1989 he received the Super Ballon d'Or, of which he is the only recipient. He helped Argentina win the [[Copa América]] in 1947, and after gaining Spanish citizenship he played for Spain, but he never appeared at the [[FIFA World Cup]]. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest footballers of all time and the greatest Real Madrid player ever.
